# Incident Report — Host Compromise, 2022-01-07

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **192.168.1.216** |
| MAC address | **9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** |
| Logged-in domain user | **SPOONWATCH\steve.smith** |
| Windows domain | SPOONWATCH.NET (DC: SPOONWATCH-DC.spoonwatch.net) |

Hostname confirmed via NTLMSSP/SMB negotiation (`DESKTOP-GXMYNO2$` machine account, frames 108–747). Domain user `steve.smith` confirmed via NTLMSSP authenticate frames (829–976) with domain field `SPOONWATCH`. MAC confirmed from Ethernet source address on all frames sourced from 192.168.1.216.

## 2. Malware Family

**Hancitor** (downloader/loader), leading to a **credential/browser-data stealer module** — attribution is **behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no IDS/AV alert files were present in the evidence set; the pcap alone was used).

Basis for the behavioral call:
- Beacon and follow-on module retrieval use POST requests to sequentially-numbered, fake `.jpg`-extension URIs under `/osk/` on a bare IP address (no DNS lookup preceded the connection — the C2 IP is hardcoded), with a `main.php` check-in — this URL/response pattern (numeric fake-image payload paths + `main.php` gate) is a well-documented Hancitor TTP.
- All requests carry `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8` and no `User-Agent` header, consistent with Hancitor's HTTP loader fingerprint.
- Seven files fetched as `.jpg` are in fact **Windows PE32 DLLs** (confirmed via `file` and hex MZ/PE headers), i.e. modules being sideloaded post-infection — Hancitor's standard role as a stager that pulls down further payloads.
- One of those DLLs subsequently harvested local Chrome/Edge data and exfiltrated it back to the same C2 in a ZIP archive (see §3), consistent with a Ficker-Stealer-style module (folder layout `autofill/`, `cc/`, `cookies/`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, `system.txt` inside a randomly-numbered `.zip`).

No malicious email/document delivery is visible in this capture — it begins mid-infection at the loader's first C2 connection, so the initial infection vector (malspam/macro) is outside the captured traffic.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### Command-and-control
- **2.56.57.108:80** (TCP) — sole C2 endpoint. No DNS query for this IP appears anywhere in the capture (hardcoded C2 address). All C2 activity occurs on one persistent TCP session (stream 65) between `20:07:32` and `20:12:18` (capture-relative), `192.168.1.216:49738 → 2.56.57.108:80`.
- Apache banner on C2: `Apache/2.4.12 (Win32) OpenSSL/1.0.1m PHP/5.3.29 mod_wsgi/4.4.11 Python/2.7.10`

### Malicious URLs (all `http://2.56.57.108`)
| URL | Direction | Content | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/osk//6.jpg` | GET-equivalent POST → download | PE32 DLL, 144,848 bytes | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| `/osk//1.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 645,592 bytes | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| `/osk//2.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 334,288 bytes | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| `/osk//3.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 137,168 bytes | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| `/osk//4.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 440,120 bytes | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| `/osk//5.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 1,246,160 bytes | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| `/osk//7.jpg` | POST → download | PE32 DLL, 83,784 bytes | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |
| `/osk//main.php` | POST (empty body, 25-byte multipart terminator) | check-in/beacon, HTTP 200 empty response | n/a |
| `/osk/` | **POST upload**, 379,629 bytes | data exfiltration (see below) | `1ecee6ff37e03c1160b8bf66d5ca8dc784e0b35fb9fd105f0964b314d310c07f` (upload body) |

All requests share request headers: `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8`, `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=1BEF0A57BE110FD467A`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, no `User-Agent`.

### Data exfiltration
The final POST to `/osk/` (frame 4816, 379,629 bytes) carries a multipart file upload:
- Filename: **`_5861695120.zip`**
- Archive contents (from string extraction of the upload body): `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `autofill/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, `system.txt`

This confirms theft of stored browser autofill data, saved payment card data, browser cookies, Outlook data, saved passwords, a desktop screenshot, and system fingerprinting information from the victim host, exfiltrated to the C2 IP.

### Malicious domains
None observed — the entire malicious C2 chain used the bare IP `2.56.57.108`, never a resolved hostname. All DNS traffic in the capture otherwise resolves to legitimate Microsoft/Windows Update infrastructure (`download.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `fe2cr.update.microsoft.com`, `settings-win.data.microsoft.com`, etc.) and internal AD SRV lookups for `spoonwatch.net` — none of which are indicators of compromise.

## 4. Summary Timeline (capture-relative)
1. `20:07:32` — TCP session opens `192.168.1.216:49738 → 2.56.57.108:80`.
2. `20:07:32`–`20:11:xx` — sequence of POSTs to `/osk//{6,1,2,3,4,5,7}.jpg`, each returning a PE32 DLL disguised with a `.jpg` extension and `Content-Type: image/jpeg`.
3. POST to `/osk//main.php` — beacon/check-in, empty response.
4. POST to `/osk/` carrying `_5861695120.zip` (379,629 bytes) — stolen browser/credential data uploaded to C2.
5. Traffic returns to background Windows Update / telemetry noise (`23.38.189.x`, `52.x.x.x` Microsoft ranges) with no further contact to `2.56.57.108`.

## 5. Recommended Actions
- Isolate `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2` (192.168.1.216) from the network immediately.
- Force a password reset for `steve.smith` and any accounts/services whose credentials could be in the exfiltrated `passwords.txt`/browser data (assume compromised: browser-saved passwords, autofill data, saved payment cards, Outlook data).
- Block `2.56.57.108` at the perimeter firewall/proxy.
- Reimage the host — Hancitor-delivered stealer payloads on a domain-joined workstation warrant a full rebuild rather than cleanup, given credential theft already completed.
- Hunt for the delivery vector (this capture starts post-infection); check mail gateway logs for malspam to this user around this timestamp, since the initial macro/document stage is not present in this pcap.
